1.pericope_label: And it came to pass, when Solomon had finished the building of the house of the Lord, and the king’s house, and all Solomon’s desire which he was pleased to do, That the Lord appeared to Solomon the second time, as he had appeared unto him at Gibeon. And the Lord said unto him, I have heard thy prayer and thy supplication, that thou hast made before me: I have hallowed this house, which thou hast built, to put my name there for ever; and mine eyes and mine heart shall be there perpetually. And if thou wilt walk before me, as David thy father walked, in integrity of heart, and in uprightness, to do according to all that I have commanded thee, and wilt keep my statutes and my judgments: Then I will establish the throne of thy kingdom upon Israel for ever, as I promised to David thy father, saying, There shall not fail thee a man upon the throne of Israel. But if ye shall at all turn from following me, ye or your children, and will not keep my commandments and my statutes which I have set before you, but go and serve other gods, and worship them: Then will I cut off Israel out of the land which I have given them; and this house, which I have hallowed for my name, will I cast out of my sight; and Israel shall be a proverb and a byword among all people: And at this house, which is high, every one that passeth by it shall be astonished, and shall hiss; and they shall say, Why hath the Lord done thus unto this land, and to this house? And they shall answer, Because they forsook the Lord their God, who brought forth their fathers out of the land of Egypt, and have taken hold upon other gods, and have worshipped them, and served them: therefore hath the Lord brought upon them all this evil.

schools.summary: Henry resolves the chronology by repunctuating, reading Solomon finished in the first verse and the Lord had appeared in the second, and dates the vision to the night after the festival. He presses the hallowing as God’s prerogative, since Solomon could dedicate but only God could hallow, and applies it to persons as living temples; he takes the entail of the blessing to pass only to those who tread in their parents’ steps, warns that the house was built to protect allegiance and not rebellion, and turns the height of the house into its moral, that it was not out of reach of judgment and its height would make its fall the more amazing.

Gill reaches the same chronological solution through the grammarians, reporting that Junius and Tremellius put the first nine verses in a parenthesis and render it for the Lord had appeared, while Piscator begins a distinct narrative. He observes that David was guilty of many failings yet never apostatized into idolatry, which is what the integrity chiefly respects, and that the Hebrew of the warning runs if in turning ye turn, meaning wholly and not in a single instance; of the last clause he offers the house of the most High, or high in esteem and fame, on a high hill and a hundred and twenty cubits tall.

Clarke makes the byword present tense, the unbelieving and stiff-necked Jew being words still in common use, and reads the whole threat as fulfilled in the destruction of the temple and the scattering of the people over the face of the earth.

Ellicott states the chronological difficulty most sharply, that the temple took seven years and the palace thirteen more and the works were successive, so that at face value the verse pushes either the dedication or the answer thirteen years past the prayer, the first infinitely improbable and contradicted by Josephus and the second more preposterous; his solution is that the notice merely summarizes the three preceding chapters. He restrains the for ever as determined by the prayer it answers, marking a settled habitation against the movable tabernacle, and alone removes the relative from the last clause, so that the true meaning is this house shall be high, as the Greek translators read and the Latin glosses as an example. Keil and Delitzsch locate the sanctifying in a fact rather than a word, that Jehovah put his name there by filling the house with the cloud which visibly displayed his presence, and trace the threat word for word to the Pentateuch, the cutting off from Deuteronomy’s curses and the desolation of the house from the curse pronounced on the land.

debates.question: How can the vision be dated when the verse speaks of all the buildings finished?

positions.view: Only as a settled habitation against the movable tabernacle; any larger sense is expressly conditional
In the fact of the cloud, by which Jehovah consecrated it as the scene of his grace
By God’s prerogative, which men cannot exercise, and which extends to persons as living temples

themes: the date of the second vision

10.pericope_label: And it came to pass at the end of twenty years, when Solomon had built the two houses, the house of the Lord, and the king’s house, (Now Hiram the king of Tyre had furnished Solomon with cedar trees and fir trees, and with gold, according to all his desire,) that then king Solomon gave Hiram twenty cities in the land of Galilee. And Hiram came out from Tyre to see the cities which Solomon had given him; and they pleased him not. And he said, What cities are these which thou hast given me, my brother? And he called them the land of Cabul unto this day. And Hiram sent to the king sixscore talents of gold.

schools.summary: Henry judges the twenty cities had not been allotted to any tribe, the border of Asher only coming up to them, but remained with the natives until Solomon mastered them. He will have neither party at fault in the quarrel over them: the country was valuable but not agreeable to Hiram’s genius, the Tyrians being merchants who lived in fine houses and grew rich by navigation and knew not how to value land fit for corn and pasture, so that a man used to the clean streets of Tyre could not agree with the miry lanes of Cabul, the best lands having commonly the worst roads through them; and he draws from it that God suits the earth’s accommodations to the dispositions of men and the dispositions of men to the earth.

Gill reckons the twenty years as the two houses together, seven for the temple and thirteen for the palace, and on the sixscore talents reads had sent, making the sum the gold already furnished for the temple and valuing it at five hundred and forty thousand pounds on one authority and nearly a million and a half ducats on another.

Clarke doubts the cities were annexed to Tyre at all, thinking Solomon gave only the produce until the loan was repaid, or else that they were heathen cities he had conquered and was free to give. On the name he says the learned are not agreed, notes a Cabul in Asher’s boundary and reports that some therefore read border, as the Greek translators did; and he makes the sixscore talents the sum Hiram had lent, to repay which Solomon taxed his people, calling the whole very darkly expressed.

Ellicott marks a literary seam here, the account of building and consecration ending at the ninth verse and what follows being brief official records markedly different in style from the graphic passages around them. He takes the cities for cities of the subject races, which Solomon would have no scruple in alienating, though the law forbidding land to be sold for ever would hardly have been strictly observed under so self-reliant a despotism; he puts Hiram’s discontent down to their condition rather than their position, canvasses Ewald’s derivation of Cabul as nought and another as like that which vanishes and objects that unless these answer to something cognate in Tyrian they hardly suit a passage implying a Phoenician origin, and warns that depreciation proves nothing, since it is naught, saith the buyer, but when he is gone his way then he boasteth. Keil and Delitzsch find the Hiram notices very imperfect, the fourteenth verse furnishing a conclusion neither in form nor substance, resolve the grammar by making the two verses one period, and gloss my brother as a conventional expression used by princes with one another.

Perhaps not given at all, but only their produce until the loan was repaid; or conquered heathen cities

Perhaps border, after the Cabul of Asher, as the Greek translators rendered it
Hebrew derivations such as as nought will not serve unless cognate in Tyrian
The gold already furnished for the temple; read had sent
The loan, to repay which Solomon taxed his people
Either a note referring back, or a payment for a cession worth more than the debt

outliers.claim: Alone in excusing both kings by temperament rather than fault, making the quarrel a difference of calling between merchant and farmer.

themes: why a Tyrian would not have them

15.pericope_label: And this is the reason of the levy which king Solomon raised; for to build the house of the Lord, and his own house, and Millo, and the wall of Jerusalem, and Hazor, and Megiddo, and Gezer. For Pharaoh king of Egypt had gone up, and taken Gezer, and burnt it with fire, and slain the Canaanites that dwelt in the city, and given it for a present unto his daughter, Solomon’s wife. And Solomon built Gezer, and Beth–horon the nether, And Baalath, and Tadmor in the wilderness, in the land, And all the cities of store that Solomon had, and cities for his chariots, and cities for his horsemen, and that which Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem, and in Lebanon, and in all the land of his dominion.

schools.summary: Henry defends the levy twice over, that Solomon was a wise builder who counted the cost first and would not begin till he could finish, and that he raised it not for war, as other princes did, spending the blood of his subjects, but for building, which required only their labour and purses. He finds the order of the works instructive, God’s house finished before his own was begun, then a house for his wife, Millo, the wall of Jerusalem, the decayed country cities, the cities of store and last Lebanon for pleasure, so that piety should begin, profit proceed and pleasure come last, for if we begin with God he will go on with us; he observes that rebuilding the country towns at his own charge made their inhabitants his tenants as well as his subjects, and of Gezer that Solomon was no warlike prince, but the king of Egypt, who was, took cities for him to build.

Gill reads the levy as both of men to work and of money to defray the expense, leaves open whether Pharaoh went up against Gezer provoked of himself or was moved to it by Solomon, who had married his daughter, and glosses the cities of store as those holding the magazines of corn, arms and ammunition.

Clarke makes the levy the tax raised to repay Hiram’s sixscore talents and calls it grievous, as we learn from the elders who came to Rehoboam begging that their yoke be lightened, adding that however plenteous silver and gold were then, the subjects must have been greatly oppressed by so vast an expenditure. He follows Calmet in making Millo a deep valley between the two hills which Solomon filled up and built on, a fortified place for public assemblies; and of Tadmor he says it is almost universally allowed to be Palmyra, quoting a description ending that the world never saw a more glorious city, the pride of ancient times and the reproach of our own, where the renowned Zenobia and the incomparable Longinus must for ever be remembered with admiration and regret.

Ellicott notes the levy fell on Israelites and subject races alike, raised first for the temple and then extended; he works Millo from the word, which seems to mean piling up, so its simplest sense is a fortified mound, notes the house of Millo at Shechem as a hint the word is Canaanitish, and reports that the Greek translators invariably render it the citadel while Josephus says only that Solomon raised David’s walls and built towers. On Tadmor he alone states the case against the received identification, that the Hebrew has Tamar, that the phrase in the land seems to mean the land of Israel and the surrounding names are southern, so the place may be the Tamar of Ezekiel or the old name of En-gedi, before yielding to the ancient versions and Josephus and granting that on that reading something has probably dropped out. Keil and Delitzsch say nothing is known of the occasion of Pharaoh’s expedition and refuse the conjecture that the city had drawn Egyptian vengeance by a raid on the coast, since by every account Gezer lay far inland; they read the written text as the palm-city with Tadmor in the margin after Chronicles, a form perhaps mere expansion yet still the name the Arabs use.

positions.view: Grievous, as the elders’ plea to Rehoboam shows, and the subjects greatly oppressed
Defensible, being raised for building and not for war, and so costing labour and purses rather than blood
Laid on Israelites and subject races alike, first for the temple and then extended
A deep valley between the hills, filled up and built on as a place for public assemblies
A fortified mound, from a word meaning piling up, rendered the citadel by the Greek translators

positions.view: Almost universally allowed to be Palmyra
The written text gives the palm-city and the margin Tadmor, which is still the name the Arabs use
The Hebrew and the southern context favour Tamar or En-gedi, though the versions and Josephus must prevail

Unclear whether he was provoked of himself or moved to it by his son-in-law

outliers.claim: Alone in arguing from the Hebrew and the southern context that the place may not be Palmyra at all, before conceding to the versions.

20.pericope_label: And all the people that were left of the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, which were not of the children of Israel, Their children that were left after them in the land, whom the children of Israel also were not able utterly to destroy, upon those did Solomon levy a tribute of bondservice unto this day. But of the children of Israel did Solomon make no bondmen: but they were men of war, and his servants, and his princes, and his captains, and rulers of his chariots, and his horsemen. These were the chief of the officers that were over Solomon’s work, five hundred and fifty, which bare rule over the people that wrought in the work. But Pharaoh’s daughter came up out of the city of David unto her house which Solomon had built for her: then did he build Millo. And three times in a year did Solomon offer burnt offerings and peace offerings upon the altar which he built unto the Lord, and he burnt incense upon the altar that was before the Lord. So he finished the house.

schools.summary: Henry supposes the remnant of the nations had renounced their idolatry and submitted, so that Solomon could not in honour destroy them, and were too poor to tax, so that he served himself of their labour, thereby observing the law that bondmen should be of the heathen and fulfilling the curse pronounced on Canaan. Of the Israelites he says they were God’s freemen, not bondmen but soldiers and courtiers holding office as they were qualified, their dignity and liberty preserved and their relation to God as a kingdom of priests honoured. On the offerings he holds that the priest burnt the incense for the king and at his charge, since to do it himself was Uzziah’s crime, and draws from the altar being one Solomon built himself that many will assist the devotions of others who neglect their own, and that whatever pains we take to support religion we are likely to have the advantage of it ourselves.

Gill grounds the Israelite exemption in law, since they might be hired servants but not bondservants, and explains the queen’s removal by the holiness of the house of David, hallowed by the ark’s having stood there, so that an Egyptian woman was not thought fit to dwell in it. On the offerings he names the three feasts and insists these were by no means the only sacrifices or the only times, since Solomon offered on sabbaths and new moons as the law of Moses commanded, and that the offering was made by the priests.

Clarke says Solomon put the subject races to the most laborious part of the public works while the Israelites were generally exempt, and sets beside it the Egyptian king who built temples throughout his country by the hands of war captives alone and had inscribed on each that no native had laboured there, remarking that Solomon might with propriety have placed a similar inscription on most of his works. On the offerings he does no more than number the three feasts.

Ellicott thinks the bondservice was not originated but only enforced and organised by Solomon, dating in theory from the Conquest with the Gibeonites for its notable instance, traces much of the danger of the stormy age of the Judges to these subject races rising, and compares the whole to medieval serfship, varying in severity by time and region. He doubts the Israelite exemption lasted, holding that however it stood in theory it must virtually have been set aside in Solomon’s later days, since the growth of the king’s absolute power might remove their condition from serfship more in name than in reality, the subject races being played off against them as the Macedonians were in Alexander’s later years; he reconciles the smaller number of officers with the larger figure elsewhere by making that a special levy and this a regular system, and states flatly that there is no reason to suppose Solomon ever personally usurped the priest’s office. Keil and Delitzsch read the two closing notices as pointing back to the third chapter and showing how the incongruities at the opening of the reign were removed by the buildings, explain that the queen came up because the palace stood on the loftier summit of Zion, and observe that the temple allowed the sacrificing on the high places to be brought to an end.

positions.view: Not originated but enforced and organised by Solomon, dating from the Conquest
A charitable alternative, since he could neither destroy nor tax them, and it kept the law
The most laborious works, for which Solomon might have earned an Egyptian king’s inscription
It was law; they might be hired but not bond servants
They were God’s freemen, made soldiers and courtiers, a kingdom of priests
Virtually set aside in his later days, serfship in name only
No; there is no reason to suppose he ever usurped the priest’s office
No; the priest burnt the incense for him, that usurpation being Uzziah’s crime
No; the offering was made by the priests

outliers.claim: Alone in turning the bondservice into a reproach, setting beside it the Egyptian temples built by captives alone and inscribed that no native had laboured there.

themes: of Israel he made no bondmen

26.pericope_label: And king Solomon made a navy of ships in Ezion–geber, which is beside Eloth, on the shore of the Red sea, in the land of Edom. And Hiram sent in the navy his servants, shipmen that had knowledge of the sea, with the servants of Solomon. And they came to Ophir, and fetched from thence gold, four hundred and twenty talents, and brought it to king Solomon.

schools.summary: Henry notes the port had belonged to the Edomites and came to the crown of Judah only by David’s conquest, and takes Ophir for the East Indies, supposing Ceylon. He draws the providence from the division of labour, Solomon sending his own servants as factors but hiring Tyrians for sailors because they had knowledge of the sea, so that one nation needs another and there may be mutual commerce; and he ends on the gold itself, that Canaan, the glory of all lands, had none in it, which teaches that the hoarding and trading part of this world’s wealth is not its best part, that Solomon’s four hundred and twenty talents were little beside David’s hundred thousand, and that the merchandise of wisdom, within reach of the poorest, is better than the merchandise of silver.

Gill reads the harbour’s name as the backbone of a man and reports that the ridge of rocks before the port lay in that form, covered at high water and standing up in points at low. He raises the difficulty that Tyrian ships could not have come from the Mediterranean without going far round, and reports the solutions offered, that Hiram kept a port of his own in the Red Sea or that the two seas were joined by a river, a notion Lightfoot censured; he observes this is the first navy of ships we read of, lists the many guesses at Ophir from Ceylon and Sofala to Peru and the Hispaniola of Columbus, who thought himself that he had found it for the gold in it, and settles with Josephus on the golden Chersonese, where a mountain near Malacca is still called Ophir.

Clarke reads the number down, the word being literally a ship, so that although Chronicles has the plural it does not appear Solomon built more than one, and that manned principally by Tyrians. On Ophir he says plainly that no man knows to this day, rejects the siting at the sources of the two rivers because the voyage required three years, and follows a traveller who placed Ophir in Sofala opposite Madagascar, where gold and silver mines have been worked from the remotest antiquity, arguing that the monsoons make three years the least possible time for the voyage.

Ellicott turns the harbour’s name into an argument, that it indicates a country which could hardly have supplied shipbuilding timber, so the ships or their materials must have come from Tyre as Chronicles says. He makes the hiring of Tyrian sailors a point about Israel’s vocation: the Tyrians were the great sailors until their own colonists and the Greeks superseded them, but Israel cared little for the sea, its coast was scantily furnished with harbours, and its call to be a separate people was absolutely incompatible with maritime commerce, so that Solomon’s venture was exceptional, with no parallel until the royal houses intermarried under Ahab and Jehoshaphat, and the Old Testament mostly regards the sea for its terrible power, declaring of the new heaven and earth that there was no more sea. On Ophir he alone separates what is certain, that it lay east of Palestine and was reached by the Red Sea and that its gold became proverbial, from what is speculation, and decides for India on the Greek and Arabic renderings, Josephus’s Golden Chersonese, and the sandal wood whose name is a corruption of the Sanscrit. Keil and Delitzsch place the harbour at the north-eastern end of the gulf and gloss Eloth as a grove, named from the palms about it, the Aila of the Greeks and Romans.
